nameStory: The Common Goldeneye gets its name from its brilliant golden-yellow eyes that seem to glow like tiny suns against its dark head. The 'clangula' part of its scientific name comes from the Latin word meaning 'to resound,' referring to the distinctive whistling sound their wings make in flight - earning them the nickname 'whistlers' among duck hunters.
description: The Common Goldeneye is a medium-sized diving duck with a distinctly rounded, bulbous head that gives it an unmistakable profile on the water. Males sport a glossy dark green head with a bright white circular patch near the bill, while females have chocolate-brown heads and grayish bodies. Both sexes flash distinctive golden eyes and show bold white wing patches when they take flight, creating a striking black-and-white pattern.

idTips.label: Golden Eyes
idTips.description: Both males and females have brilliant golden-yellow eyes that catch the light like amber jewels - visible even at a distance through binoculars

idTips.label: Rounded Head Shape
idTips.description: The head appears distinctly bulbous and rounded, almost triangular in profile, giving the bird a 'big-headed' appearance that's quite different from other ducks

idTips.label: Male's White Face Patch
idTips.description: Adult males display a bright white oval or circular patch between the eye and bill against their iridescent dark green head - like a white spotlight

idTips.label: Wing Whistle
idTips.description: Listen for a distinctive whistling or singing sound when they fly - their wing feathers create this musical note that carries across the water

idTips.label: Diving Behavior
idTips.description: Watch them disappear completely underwater with a quick forward dive, staying submerged for 20-30 seconds while searching for food on the bottom

habitat: Common Goldeneyes prefer deeper, open waters throughout New England, including large lakes, rivers, coastal bays, and harbors. During winter, they're often found in saltwater areas like protected coves and estuaries, while in migration they use inland lakes and reservoirs. They need clear water deep enough for diving, typically 6-10 feet or more.

seasonality.spring: Peak migration occurs in March and April when flocks move through on their way to northern breeding grounds. Males display their elaborate courtship behaviors with head-throwing and calling.
seasonality.summer: Most birds have moved north to breed, though a few non-breeding individuals may linger in northern New England. This is the least likely season to spot them.
seasonality.fall: Return migration begins in October and November, with birds appearing on larger lakes and coastal waters. Both adults and young-of-the-year can be observed.
seasonality.winter: Peak abundance occurs from December through February, especially along the coast and on ice-free inland waters. This is the best time to observe their striking winter plumage.

funFact: Common Goldeneye ducklings make one of the most dramatic entrances into the world - they leap from tree cavities up to 50 feet high just one day after hatching, bouncing like tiny feathered ping-pong balls when they hit the ground before following their mother to water!
confusionNotes: Female Common Goldeneyes can be confused with female Redheads or Ring-necked Ducks, but remember 'golden eyes, round head' - the bright yellow eyes and distinctly bulbous head shape are dead giveaways. Buffleheads are much smaller with different head patterns, while Barrow's Goldeneyes are extremely rare in New England.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'sea duck,' Common Goldeneyes are equally at home on freshwater lakes and rivers. The genus name 'Bucephala' means 'bullheaded' in Greek, referring to their distinctive rounded skull shape that helps distinguish all goldeneyes and buffleheads from other ducks.
compareHints: Common Goldeneyes are much larger than their Bufflehead cousins and have different head patterns - males lack the Bufflehead's white head patch that wraps around the back of the head. The extremely rare Barrow's Goldeneye male has a crescent-shaped (not round) white face patch and more black on the back, while females are nearly impossible to distinguish in the field.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Buffleheads are much smaller than their goldeneye cousins and have that distinctive puffy, rounded head shape.
Compared to Common Goldeneye, Barrow's has a more triangular white face patch, steeper forehead, and slightly larger overall size.
